passages.title: Christ's place above every power supports the hearers' received hope
passages.summary: Paul and Timothy write to the saints at Colossae. They thank God for the faith of readers whom Epaphras taught. They pray that the readers be filled with knowledge of God’s will. The Father moved them from darkness into the kingdom of his Son. A passage of praise follows. The Son is God’s image, and all things were created through him. He is head of the body, and through him God reconciles all things. Paul rejoices in his sufferings and labors to present everyone mature in Christ.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the cities the letter names. They do not show homes or the place where Paul is held.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson studies faith strengthened through Christ's saving work. Why does the account of Christ's place support the hearers' received hope?

contextNote.title: Christ's place above every power supports the hearers' received hope
contextNote.text: Verse 16 says all things were created through the Son. It lists them: things in heaven and on earth, thrones and powers. Verse 20 uses the same range for reconciliation. God reconciles all things, on earth and in the heavens. The means is stated without softening: peace through the blood of his cross. Verses 21–22 apply it to the readers. They were once alienated, and now he has reconciled them.

passages.title: The joined body grows through its head rather than added claims to special wisdom
passages.summary: Paul says he struggles for the readers and for those at Laodicea. All the treasures of wisdom are hidden in Christ. They should walk in him as they were taught. He warns against philosophy and empty deceit built on human tradition. In Christ all the fullness of deity lives in bodily form. God forgave them and nailed the record of debt to the cross. No one should judge them about food, festivals, new moons, or Sabbaths. Rules like “Don’t handle, nor taste, nor touch” have no value against the flesh.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the cities the letter names. They do not show homes or the place where Paul is held.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches remaining rooted in Christ against deceptive influences. How does holding the head differ from depending on added rules?

contextNote.title: The joined body grows through its head rather than added claims to special wisdom
contextNote.text: Verse 18 describes a person who would rob the readers of their prize. He insists on false humility and the worship of angels. Verse 19 names what is wrong with him. He does not hold firmly to the Head. The body grows only from there, and the growth is God’s. Verse 10 has already said the readers are made full in Christ. So verses 20–23 ask why they submit to added rules.

passages.title: Received new life requires changed speech and care within still unequal households
passages.summary: Paul says the readers were raised with Christ and should seek the things above. Their life is hidden with Christ in God. They are to put to death immorality, greed, anger, and lying. In the new man there is no Greek or Jew, slave or free. They are to put on compassion, kindness, and patience, and to forgive. Love binds all together, and Christ’s peace should rule. Instructions follow for wives, husbands, children, fathers, and servants. Whatever they do, they are to do it as for the Lord.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the cities the letter names. They do not show homes or the place where Paul is held.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches putting away former conduct and practicing shared care. How does seeking what is above change conduct toward earthly neighbors?

contextNote.title: Received new life requires changed speech and care within still unequal households
contextNote.text: Verses 8–9 use the picture of clothing: put away anger, malice, and lying. Verse 10 says they have put on the new man. Verse 12 tells them what the new clothing is. It first names who they are: God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved. The five garments all concern other people: compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance. Verse 13 adds forgiving one another as Christ forgave. Verse 14 puts love over all of it as the bond.

passages.title: Letters, messengers, and prayer connect separate assemblies with the chained speaker
passages.summary: Masters are told to give their servants what is just and equal. Paul asks for prayer that a door will open for the word. He is in chains for it. He sends Tychicus and Onesimus to report his news. Aristarchus, Mark, Jesus called Justus, Epaphras, Luke, and Demas send greetings. He greets the brothers in Laodicea and the assembly in the house of Nymphas. The letter is to be read in Laodicea too. Paul signs with his own hand and asks them to remember his chains.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the cities the letter names. They do not show homes or the place where Paul is held.

lds.text: Why do personal messengers matter beside the request to exchange letters?

contextNote.title: Letters, messengers, and prayer connect separate assemblies with the chained speaker
contextNote.text: Paul cannot visit; he is in chains (verses 3 and 18). The letter stands in for him, and people carry it. Verses 7–9 send Tychicus and Onesimus to tell what the letter does not. Verse 16 then orders two public readings. This letter is to be read at Colossae and at Laodicea. A letter from Laodicea is to be read at Colossae in exchange. The verse shows these letters were written to be heard by whole assemblies.
